claims.statement: The Aho-Corasick finite-state machine improves the repeated single-pattern scan for multi-keyword bibliographic search.
The inspected Gitleaks prefilter is implemented with a library explicitly implementing Aho-Corasick.
The current Bateia component mechanically resembles a repeated single-pattern scan.
The current Bateia component is historically and mechanically derived from the Aho-Corasick automaton.
The Bateia component was influenced by the Gitleaks Aho-Corasick prefilter.

bases.summary: The original paper contrasts its finite-state machine with straightforward matching, reports text processing independent of the number of keywords, and reports a five-to-tenfold improvement on typical bibliographic inputs.
The improvement follows from sharing prefix states and failure transitions instead of restarting an independent search for every keyword.
The detector imports github.com/BobuSumisu/aho-corasick, constructs its trie, and calls Match on decoded text as a prefilter.
MatchAll iterates over every stored pattern and invokes strings.Contains separately for each one; the type stores no automaton states or failure links.
The official Go source defines strings.Contains as Index(s, substr) >= 0, confirming that each Bateia loop iteration launches a standalone substring lookup.
The design prompt explicitly names Aho-Corasick and requests construction of its multiple-pattern automaton with O(n+m) behavior.
The delivered component keeps the historical name but implements a per-pattern strings.Contains loop, so the available artifact does not establish mechanical descent from the finite-state algorithm.
The Bateia prompt says the component was discovered during a scan that included gitleaks/gitleaks.
The inspected Gitleaks artifact proves use of an Aho-Corasick library but contains no reference to Bateia and cannot by itself establish a direct transfer path.
